cards.text: This one's a psalm of Asaph, the chief of the Levites King David appointed to praise the LORD (1 Chronicles 16:4-5). And Asaph skips the small talk. No hello, no how's the weather, he cries out to God, OUT LOUD, so God will hear him.

cards.question: Asaph is in a day of trouble, seeking the Lord. All through the night, his outstretched hands grow weary.
In his day of trouble, how does Asaph's soul respond to comfort?

cards.text: So Asaph turns his thoughts to God Himself. You'd think this is where the sun comes out and the birds start singing.

cards.question: When Asaph remembers God in his trouble, what happens to him?

answers.text: He groans and his spirit grows faint
He sings and his spirit grows strong
He rests and his spirit grows calm

cards.text: And sleep? Asaph tells God He's kept his eyes from closing, so now Asaph's up all night, lying there, supervising the ceiling.

cards.question: Up all night, Asaph is so ___ that he can't even speak.

cards.text: Too troubled to speak. Friend, my first stretch in that junk drawer I barely said a WORD, and now look at me, you can't get me to STOP!
So Asaph thinks back to the days of old, the years long in the past. At night he remembers his song, and his spirit starts asking some hard questions.

cards.question: In the night, Asaph's spirit starts asking hard questions. What is he afraid might last forever?

answers.text: The Lord turning away from His people
His own nights without any sleep

cards.question: In his questions, Asaph even wonders if God's promise has failed for all time.
Asaph wonders if God has forgotten to be gracious, and if God's anger has shut off His ___.
After all those questions, Asaph sums up his grief in one line. What does he say has changed?

answers.text: The right hand of the Most High
The hearts of the people of Israel
The song he sang in the night

cards.text: That's the bottom of the valley for Asaph, friend: questions everywhere, answers nowhere. But stay with me, because this psalm is NOT done.
Then the whole psalm turns on one little word: will. Asaph quits supervising the ceiling and finally flips on the light.

cards.question: After all his hard questions, Asaph decides to ___ the works of the LORD.
Asaph plans to take a quick glance at what God has done and move right along.

cards.text: And listen to how his voice changes. Asaph tells God that His way is holy.

cards.question: Asaph asks God a question again, but a very different kind than before. Which one?

answers.text: What god is so great as our God
How long will this night go on
Why have You left us all alone

cards.text: He calls God the One who works wonders and shows His strength among the peoples. Ten verses ago this man was too troubled to talk, and now he's the loudest guy in the STADIUM.

cards.question: Asaph says God redeemed His people with power. Who are they?

answers.text: The sons of Jacob and Joseph
The sons of Moab and Ammon
The sons of Esau and Ishmael

cards.text: Now Asaph stops talking about God's wonders and starts painting one. And it starts with water.

cards.question: In Asaph's picture, what do the waters do when they see God?

answers.text: They swirl and even the depths shake
They freeze and the depths stand still
They rise and cover the whole land

cards.text: Then the sky joins in: clouds pour down water, thunder resounds, and God's arrows flash back and forth. I bet it sounded like every oven door in my bakery slamming shut at ONCE.

cards.question: With God's thunder resounding in the whirlwind, the earth stays perfectly still.

cards.text: The lightning lights up the world, and the whole earth trembles and quakes. Meanwhile me? I used to jump when somebody rattled the junk drawer looking for TAPE.

cards.question: God's path led through the sea, His way through the mighty waters, and His footprints were plain for anyone to see.

cards.text: A path you can walk, but no footprints you can find. I think that's Asaph's whole long night in one line: God was at work even when Asaph couldn't see a trace of Him.

cards.question: God's footprints can't be found, but He still leads. How does He lead His people?

answers.text: Like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron
Like an army by the hand of Joshua and Caleb
Like a nation by the hand of David and Solomon

cards.text: Moses and Aaron, the two the LORD told to bring the Israelites out of Egypt (Exodus 6:26). The man who started this psalm too troubled to speak ends it remembering God leading His people like a flock.

findings.problem: This true or false card asks whether Asaph's outstretched hands grow weary through the night. No earlier card gives any context the baker could reason from. The natural guess (True) is the trap, so the baker can only get it right by luck. It also tests the exact wording of the line ('did not grow weary') rather than its meaning.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: The setup line 'You'd think this is where the sun comes out and the birds start singing' signals that the opposite happens. That rules out both wrong answers on card 5 ('He sings and his spirit grows strong' and 'He rests and his spirit grows calm'), so the baker can pick the right answer without reasoning from the psalm.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: This story card repeats verse 4 ('Too troubled to speak'), which card 6 told and card 7 already asked. It then adds only a joke. It doesn't move the baker forward through the passage, so it works as a recap card. The joke should ride along on a card that tells new text.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.

findings.problem: The question states 'What is he afraid might last forever?' This presents Asaph's fear as fact. Verse 7 only gives his question ('Will the Lord spurn us forever…'). The feeling is not marked as a guess.

rule.text: Feelings: He can guess at a feeling, marked as his own ("I think," "I bet"). Never as fact.

findings.problem: This fill in the blank repeats verse 9 almost word for word and blanks its last word ('Has His anger shut off His ___'). The baker is guessing the next word of a line of poetry rather than reasoning about its meaning.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: This card cites Psalm 77:10 but tells nothing from verse 10, which card 13 already covered. It sums up the stop ('questions everywhere, answers nowhere') and teases what's ahead, so it is a recap card rather than one that moves the passage forward. Its citation also doesn't match what it tells.

The question says Asaph asks 'a very different kind than before.' Both wrong answers ('How long will this night go on' and 'Why have You left us all alone') are the same kind of question as before. Card 4's 'listen to how his voice changes' points the same way. The wording rules out the wrong answers.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: 'the whole earth trembles and quakes' adds 'whole'. Verse 18 says only 'the earth trembled and quaked.' This line is a statement of the text, not part of the joke.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: 'The man who started this psalm too troubled to speak' is not true to the text. Asaph starts the psalm crying aloud to God (Psalm 77:1). He becomes too troubled to speak in verse 4.

rule.text: Noticing: What he points out must be true.
